`/Users/kenneth/jusprin-win-vm-harness/BUILDING.md`; VM setup in its README.
See [[windows-gui-test-vm-gcp]].

**Why:** four of the five failures below produce misleading errors far from
their cause, and two were self-inflicted by how the build was driven.

**How to apply:**
- Run long builds as a Windows **scheduled task** (SYSTEM / ServiceAccount), not
  over SSH — OpenSSH kills the process tree on disconnect. Never let two builds
  share a directory: that produced OpenSSL `C1033 cannot open program database`.
- Add `C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin` to PATH so **awk** is found, or libpng
  cannot generate `pngprefix.h` (`-DPNG_PREFIX=` in deps/PNG/PNG.cmake) and you
  get a confusing `C1083` on a header that was never written.
- Set `CMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5` for CMake 4.x.
- **Do not use the CI deps artifact** — the shipped bundle predates `deps/Eigen`
  and cannot satisfy Eigen 5.0.1. Build deps from source.
- Never hard-stop the VM mid-build: doing so left 622 installed files full of
  NUL bytes and surfaced as fake syntax errors inside Boost headers.
- Qhull is deliberately excluded on MSVC (deps/CMakeLists.txt), so 24/25 is
  complete on Windows.
- To run headless, use the app's own hook rather than dropping DLLs beside the
  exe: `src/OrcaSlicer_app_msvc.cpp` loads `<exedir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` when
  system OpenGL < 2.0. Still force `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe`.

The `Build all` Windows CI job fails at `cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022"` with
"could not find any instance of Visual Studio". That is a GitHub runner
environment problem, not `build_release_vs.bat` — the same script selects the
same generator on the VM and configures fine against registered Build Tools.

**MSVC rejects `this` in a nested lambda's init-capture.** Found 2026-09-07 at
commit fbe5963b: `CallAfter([self=wxWeakRef<wxWindow>(this),...])` written INSIDE
another lambda compiled on clang but failed on MSVC with 37 errors, because MSVC
bound that `this` to the enclosing closure object, so it tried to build a
`wxWeakRef<wxWindow>` from a lambda pointer
(`Tracked_class_should_inherit_from_wxTrackable`). Name the object first —
`auto* menu = this;` then capture `menu`. Watch for this pattern whenever a
deferred callback is set up from within another lambda; it is invisible on macOS.

content.text:
No, and this is worth being precise about, because the opposite is true.

**What a restorable copy is.** It is a complete project 3MF written fresh from the in-memory model: every mesh, every object and plate, the per-object settings, painting data, and the printer, filament and process configuration, plus rendered plate thumbnails. Nothing in it is a byte-for-byte copy of anything on disk. The export re-encodes every triangle as XML text and compresses it each time, which is exactly why it costs 0.8 s for a 20 MB mesh.

**What is left out.** The one thing the copy skips is the project's auxiliary folder, which is where JusPrin's own data lives, including earlier copies. The adapter's comment says so directly: the auxiliary skip "keeps consumer files (and earlier checkpoints) out of the archive," and the exporter honors that flag when it walks the auxiliary directory ([bbs_3mf.cpp:8555](src/libslic3r/Format/bbs_3mf.cpp:8555)).

**Where it goes.** Each copy is stored inside the project's auxiliary folder under a JusPrin subfolder, in a revisions directory, named by revision id with a snapshot suffix ([ProjectPersistence.cpp:125](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectPersistence.cpp:125)). So the JusPrin subfolder is where copies are kept, not what they contain.

**Why a straight copy of the project file would not work anyway.** The point of a copy is to capture unsaved edits at a conversation boundary. The project file on disk only reflects the last explicit save, so copying its bytes would restore the wrong state. That is also why the cost cannot be dodged by copying files; the meshes have to be serialized from memory, and the only lever is doing that off the UI thread, which is what the copy-cost handoff proposes.

If you had a different scheme in mind, where the meshes stay in one shared file and each revision stores only what changed, that would be a new design. It is not what the code does today and not what either handoff describes.

Let me trace both halves in the code before answering: how a revert restores a copy, and whether copies survive a save and reopen.

content.text:
Restorability works the same way today and in the design: a revert throws away the in-memory project and loads a saved copy as if it were a project file. What differs is how many copies exist. Here is the full path, then your move-and-rotate scenario.

**How a revert restores.** `restore_project_archive` ([OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:396](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:396)) resets the Plater, loads the copy with the model-and-config strategy, and clears OrcaSlicer's undo stack. Because the copy is a complete project, everything comes back with it: object positions and rotations, plates, painting, per-object and global settings. Before the load, persistence copies the surviving checkpoints to a scratch directory, since the old auxiliary folder is destroyed by the project replacement, and copies them back afterwards ([ProjectPersistence.cpp:392](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectPersistence.cpp:392)).

**How copies survive save and reopen.** Copies and `state.json` live in the project's auxiliary folder under a JusPrin subfolder. When you save the project, OrcaSlicer embeds the whole auxiliary folder into the 3MF, so every checkpoint travels inside the saved file. On reopen, OrcaSlicer extracts the auxiliary folder to a temporary directory, persistence finds `state.json` there and adopts it, and every revision that still has a file is revertible ([ProjectPersistence.cpp:204](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectPersistence.cpp:204)). OrcaSlicer's own undo stack is memory-only and is empty after reopen. So after reopen, JusPrin's copies are the only restore points.

**Your scenario, in today's code.** Each move or rotate fires a Transform notification and writes a copy synchronously. Save, reopen, and every one of those moves has its own "Revert here". The price is one full export per drag.

**Your scenario, in the design.** A move or rotate writes a change log entry only. A copy is taken at the next conversation item. After save and reopen, the timeline still shows the moves, because the log is in `state.json`, and you can revert to the state at any conversation boundary. You cannot revert to a point between two moves, and moves made after the last message are simply the live state. Within a session OrcaSlicer's Undo covers those steps; after reopen it does not. This is the accepted D4 trade-off, and it is sharper after reopen. If that matters, the only lever is the copy trigger, for example also taking a copy on save when entries exist since the last one.

**Two conditions to be aware of.** Copies exist only after you save: if the project is closed without saving, the temporary auxiliary folder goes with it, and I would expect the checkpoints to go too. And there is no pruning: every copy is kept forever and re-embedded on every save. At today's measured sizes, a project with a 20 MB mesh grows by 4.6 MB per checkpoint, and the save re-compresses all of them. That growth is not in either handoff and belongs in the copy-cost one as a second consequence of the same number.

What do you mean by copies?  Define copies in plain English.  Use the styogram to help me understand conceptually what happens when rotate is performed and how close and reopening the project will work as expected.

3. Find your rightmost element: max(x + width) across all rects. All content must stay within x=0 to x=680.
4. For text with text-anchor="end", the text extends LEFT from x. If x=118 and text is 200px wide, it starts at x=-82 — outside the viewBox. Increase x or use text-anchor="start".
5. Never use negative x or y coordinates. The viewBox starts at 0,0.
6. **No unintentional overlaps.** For every pair of elements that aren't meant to layer (label-on-label, label-on-arrow, box-on-box, callout-on-shape), check their bounding boxes do not intersect. The only allowed overlaps are deliberate: a label centered inside its own box, an arrowhead touching the box it points to, a highlight rect behind the thing it highlights. If two unrelated elements would collide, move one — shorten the label, shift the y, add a row. A diagram with crossed labels reads as broken regardless of how good the content is.
7. Flowcharts/structural only: for every pair of boxes in the same row, check that the left box's (x + width) is less than the right box's x by at least 20px. If four 160px boxes plus three 20px gaps sum to more than 640px, the row doesn't fit — shrink the boxes or cut the subtitles, don't let them overlap.

**SVG setup**: `<svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 680 H" role="img"><title>…</title><desc>…</desc>…` — 680px wide, flexible height. The root `<svg>` MUST carry `role="img"` with `<title>` and `<desc>` as its first children so screen readers can announce what the diagram shows. Set H to fit content tightly — the last element's bottom edge + 40px padding. Don't leave excess empty space below the content. Safe area: x=40 to x=640, y=40 to y=(H-40). Background transparent. **Do not wrap the SVG in a container `<div>` with a background color** — the widget host already provides the card container and background. Output the raw `<svg>` element directly.

**The 680 in viewBox is load-bearing — do not change it.** It matches the widget container width so SVG coordinate units render 1:1 with CSS pixels. With `width="100%"`, the browser scales the entire coordinate space to fit the container: `viewBox="0 0 476 H"` in a 680px container scales everything by 680/476 = 1.43×, so your `class="th"` 14px text renders at ~20px. The font calibration table below and all "text fits in box" math assume 1:1. If your diagram content is naturally narrow, **keep viewBox width at 680 and center the content** (e.g. content spans x=240..440) — do not shrink the viewBox to hug the content. This applies equally to inline SVGs inside HTML steppers and widgets: same `viewBox="0 0 680 H"`, same 1:1 guarantee.

**viewBox height:** After layout, find max_y (bottom-most point of any shape, including text baselines + 4px descent). Set viewBox height = max_y + 20. Don't guess.

**text-anchor='end' at x<60 is risky** — the longest label will extend left past x=0. Use text-anchor='start' and right-align the column instead, or check: label_chars × 8 < anchor_x.

**One SVG per tool call** — each call must contain exactly one <svg> element. Never leave an abandoned or partial SVG in the output. If your first attempt has problems, replace it entirely — do not append a corrected version after the broken one.

**Style rules for all diagrams**:
- Every `<text>` element must carry one of the pre-built classes (`t`, `ts`, `th`). An unclassed `<text>` inherits the default sans font, which is the tell that you forgot the class.
- Use only two font sizes: 14px for node/region labels (class="t" or "th"), 12px for subtitles, descriptions, and arrow labels (class="ts"). No other sizes.
- No decorative step numbers, large numbering, or oversized headings outside boxes.
- No icons or illustrations inside boxes — text only. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use simple shape-based indicators inside drawn objects — see below.)
- Sentence case on all labels.

**Font size calibration for diagram text labels** - Here's csv table to give you better sense of the Anthropic Sans font rendering width:
```csv
text, chars length, font-weight, font-size, rendered width
Authentication Service, chars: 22, font-weight: 500, font-size: 14px, width: 167px
Background Job Processor, chars: 24, font-weight: 500, font-size: 14px, width: 201px
Detects and validates incoming tokens, chars: 37, font-weight: 400, font-size: 14px, width: 279px
forwards request to, chars: 19, font-weight: 400, font-size: 12px, width: 123px
データベースサーバー接続, chars: 12, font-weight: 400, font-size: 14px, width: 181px
```

Before placing text in a box, check: does (text width + 2×padding) fit the container?

**SVG `<text>` never auto-wraps.** Every line break needs an explicit `<tspan x="..." dy="1.2em">`. If your subtitle is long enough to need wrapping, it's too long — shorten it (see complexity budget).

**Example check**: You want to put "Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)" in a rounded rect. The text is 20 characters at 14px ≈ 180px wide. Add 2×24px padding = 228px minimum box width. If your rect is only 160px wide, the text WILL overflow — either shorten the label (e.g. just "Glucose") or widen the box. Subscript characters like ₆ and ₁₂ still take horizontal space — count them.

**Pre-built classes** (already loaded in SVG widget):
- `class="t"` = sans 14px primary, `class="ts"` = sans 12px secondary, `class="th"` = sans 14px medium (500)
- `class="box"` = neutral rect (`--surface-1` fill, `--border-strong` stroke)
- `class="node"` = clickable group with hover effect (cursor pointer, slight dim on hover)
- `class="arr"` = arrow line (1.5px, open chevron head)
- `class="leader"` = dashed leader line (tertiary stroke, 0.5px, dashed)
- `class="c-{ramp}"` = colored node (c-blue, c-teal, c-amber, c-green, c-red, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink, c-gray). Apply to `<g>` or shape element (rect/circle/ellipse), NOT to paths. Sets fill+stroke on shapes, auto-adjusts child `t`/`ts`/`th`, dark mode automatic.

**c-{ramp} nesting:** These classes use direct-child selectors (`>`). Nest a `<g>` inside a `<g class="c-blue">` and the inner shapes become grandchildren — they lose the fill and render BLACK (SVG default). Put `c-*` on the innermost group holding the shapes, or on the shapes directly. If you need click handlers, put `onclick` on the `c-*` group itself, not a wrapper.

- Short aliases: `var(--p)`, `var(--s)`, `var(--t)`, `var(--bg2)`, `var(--b)`
- Arrow marker: always include this `<defs>` at the start of every SVG:
  `<defs><marker id="arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M2 1L8 5L2 9" fill="none" stroke="context-stroke" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/></marker></defs>`
  Then use `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` on lines. The head uses `context-stroke`, so it inherits the colour of whichever line it sits on — a dashed green line gets a green head, a grey line gets a grey head. Never a colour mismatch. Do not add filters or extra markers to `<defs>`. `<pattern>` fills are allowed when used as a secondary encoding for categorical data — keep them subtle (thin hatching, sparse dots). Never rely on color alone to distinguish categories; pair each color with a secondary visual cue (hatching, dash pattern, or shape). Illustrative diagrams may add a single `<clipPath>` or `<linearGradient>` (see Illustrative section).

**Minimize standalone labels.** Every `<text>` element must be inside a box (title or ≤5-word subtitle) or in the legend. Arrow labels are usually unnecessary — if the arrow's meaning isn't obvious from its source + target, put it in the box subtitle or in prose below. Labels floating in space collide with things and are ambiguous.

**Stroke width:** Use 0.5px strokes for diagram borders and edges — not 1px or 2px. Thin strokes feel more refined.

**Connector paths need `fill="none"`.** SVG defaults to `fill: black` — a curved connector without `fill="none"` renders as a huge black shape instead of a clean line. Every `<path>` or `<polyline>` used as a connector/arrow MUST have `fill="none"`. Only set fill on shapes meant to be filled (rects, circles, polygons).

**Rect rounding:** `rx="4"` for subtle corners. `rx="8"` max for emphasized rounding. `rx` ≥ half the height = pill shape — deliberate only.

**Schematic containers use dashed rects with a label.** Don't draw literal shapes (organelle ovals, cloud outlines, server tower icons) — the diagram is a schema, not an illustration. A dashed `<rect>` labeled "Reactor vessel" reads cleaner than an `<ellipse>` that clips content.

**Lines stop at component edges.** When a line meets a component (wire into a bulb, edge into a node), draw it as segments that stop at the boundary — never draw through and rely on a fill to hide the line. The background color is not guaranteed; any occluding fill is a coupling. Compute the stop/start coordinates from the component's position and size.

**Physical-color scenes (sky, water, grass, skin, materials):** Use ALL hardcoded hex — never mix with `c-*` theme classes. The scene should not invert in dark mode. If you need a dark variant, key it on the app theme: `[data-mode="dark"] .scene` for the normal case, plus `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-mode]) .scene }` as the OS fallback for when no app theme was provided (the widget root carries `data-mode`; a bare media query alone would follow the OS even when the claude.ai setting disagrees) — this is the one place dark variants for hardcoded colors are allowed. Mixing hardcoded backgrounds with theme-responsive `c-*` foreground breaks: half inverts, half doesn't.

**No rotated text**. `<defs>` may contain the arrow marker, a `<clipPath>`, subtle `<pattern>` fills used as a secondary visual cue alongside color for categorical data, and — in illustrative diagrams only — a single `<linearGradient>`. Nothing else: no filters, no extra markers.


## Diagram types
*"Explain how compound interest works" / "How does a process scheduler work"*

**Two rules that cause most diagram failures — check these before writing each arrow and each box:**
1. **Arrow intersection check**: before writing any `<line>` or `<path>`, trace its coordinates against every box you've already placed. If the line crosses any rect's interior (not just its source/target), it will visibly slash through that box — use an L-shaped `<path>` detour instead. This applies to arrows crossing labels too.
2. **Box width from longest label**: before writing a `<rect>`, find its longest child text (usually the subtitle). `rect_width = max(title_chars × 8, subtitle_chars × 7) + 24`. A 100px-wide box holds at most a 10-char subtitle. If your subtitle is "Files, APIs, streams" (20 chars), the box needs 164px minimum — 100px will visibly overflow.

**Tier packing:** Compute total width BEFORE placing. Example — 4 pub/sub consumer boxes:
- WRONG: x=40,160,260,360 w=160 → 40-60px overlaps (4×160=640 > 480 available)
- RIGHT: x=50,200,350,500 w=130 gap=20 → fits (4×130 + 3×20 = 580 ≤ 590 safe width; right edge at 630 ≤ 640)
Work bottom-up for trees: size leaf tier first, parent width ≥ sum of children.

**Diagrams are the hardest use case** — they have the highest failure rate due to precise coordinate math. Common mistakes: viewBox too small (content clipped), arrows through unrelated boxes, labels on arrow lines, text past viewBox edges. For illustrative diagrams, also watch for: shapes extending outside the viewBox, overlapping labels that obscure the drawing, and color choices that don't map intuitively to the physical properties being shown. Double-check coordinates before finalizing.

Use SVG for diagrams. The widget automatically wraps SVG output in a card.

**Pick the right diagram type.** The decision is about *intent*, not subject matter. Ask: is the user trying to *document* this, or *understand* it?

**Reference diagrams** — the user wants a map they can point at. Precision matters more than feeling. Boxes, labels, arrows, containment. These are the diagrams you'd find in documentation.
- **Flowchart** — steps in sequence, decisions branching, data transforming. Good for: approval workflows, request lifecycles, build pipelines, "what happens when I click submit". Trigger phrases: *"walk me through the process"*, *"what are the steps"*, *"what's the flow"*.
- **Structural diagram** — things inside other things. Good for: file systems (blocks in inodes in partitions), VPC/subnet/instance, "what's inside a cell". Trigger phrases: *"what's the architecture"*, *"how is this organised"*, *"where does X live"*.

**Intuition diagrams** — the user wants to *feel* how something works. The goal isn't a correct map, it's the right mental model. These should look nothing like a flowchart. The subject doesn't need a physical form — it needs a *visual metaphor*.
- **Illustrative diagram** — draw the mechanism. Physical things get cross-sections (water heaters, engines, lungs). Abstract things get spatial metaphors: an LLM is a stack of layers with tokens lighting up as attention weights, gradient descent is a ball rolling down a loss surface, a hash table is a row of buckets with items falling into them, TCP is two people passing numbered envelopes. Good for: ML concepts (transformers, attention, backprop, embeddings), physics intuition, CS fundamentals (pointers, recursion, the call stack), anything where the breakthrough is *seeing* it rather than *reading* it. Trigger phrases: *"how does X actually work"*, *"explain X"*, *"I don't get X"*, *"give me an intuition for X"*.

**Route on the verb, not the noun.** Same subject, different diagram depending on what was asked:

| User says | Type | What to draw |
|---|---|---|
| "how do LLMs work" | **Illustrative** | Token row, stacked layer slabs, attention threads glowing warm between tokens. Go interactive if you can. |
| "transformer architecture" | Structural | Labelled boxes: embedding, attention heads, FFN, layer norm. |
| "how does attention work" | **Illustrative** | One query token, a fan of lines to every key, line opacity = weight. |
| "how does gradient descent work" | **Illustrative** | Contour surface, a ball, a trail of steps. Slider for learning rate. |
| "what are the training steps" | Flowchart | Forward → loss → backward → update. Boxes and arrows. |
| "how does TCP work" | **Illustrative** | Two endpoints, numbered packets in flight, an ACK returning. |
| "TCP handshake sequence" | Flowchart | SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Three boxes. |
| "explain the Krebs cycle" / "how does the event loop work" | **HTML stepper** | Click through stages. Never a ring. |
| "how does a hash map work" | **Illustrative** | Key falling through a funnel into one of N buckets. |
| "draw the database schema" / "show me the ERD" | **mermaid.js** | `erDiagram` syntax. Not SVG. |

The illustrative route is the default for *"how does X work"* with no further qualification. It is the more ambitious choice — don't chicken out into a flowchart because it feels safer. Claude draws these well.

Don't mix families in one diagram. If you need both, draw the intuition version first (build the mental model), then the reference version (fill in the precise labels) as a second tool call with prose between.

**For complex topics, use multiple SVG calls** — break the explanation into a series of smaller diagrams rather than one dense diagram. Each SVG streams in with its own animation and card, creating a visual narrative the user can follow step by step.

**Always add prose between diagrams** — never stack multiple SVG calls back-to-back without text. Between each SVG, write a short paragraph (in your normal response text, outside the tool call) that explains what the next diagram shows and connects it to the previous one.

**Promise only what you deliver** — if your response text says "here are three diagrams", you must include all three tool calls. Never promise a follow-up diagram and omit it. If you can only fit one diagram, adjust your text to match. One complete diagram is better than three promised and one delivered.

#### Flowchart

For sequential processes, cause-and-effect, decision trees.

**Planning**: Size boxes to fit their text generously. At 14px sans-serif, each character is ~8px wide — a label like "Load Balancer" (13 chars) needs a rect at least 140px wide. When in doubt, make boxes wider and leave more space between them. Cramped diagrams are the most common failure mode.

**Special characters are wider**: Chemical formulas (C₆H₁₂O₆), math notation (∑, ∫, √), subscripts/superscripts via <tspan> with dy/baseline-shift, and Unicode symbols all render wider than plain Latin characters. For labels containing formulas or special notation, add 30-50% extra width to your estimate. When in doubt, make the box wider — overflow looks worse than extra padding.

content.text:
Reading the diagram top to bottom:

**The two rotates before the message** each write only a log entry. Nothing is copied. While the session is open, OrcaSlicer's own Undo can step back through them, so nothing is lost.

**Sending the message** is the moment a copy is taken. Copy r-2 is the whole project as it stands after both rotates. From here on, r-2 is a permanent restore point.

**The third rotate** after the message is the important case. It writes a log entry but no copy, because no message has been sent since. It is the live state of the project, which is fine while the session is open.

**Save and close** writes the project file with three things inside: the model as it is right now, including the third rotate; the change log; and the two copies r-1 and r-2. The third rotate is saved as the current state of the model, so nothing is lost by closing.

**Reopen** unpacks that folder, so the timeline shows all three rotates and both restore points are available. The only thing gone is OrcaSlicer's Undo, which never survives a reopen. So after reopen you can get back to the state before the third rotate by reverting to the message, and you can get back to the very start with r-1, but you cannot step back through the first two rotates one at a time.

**Revert here** on the message loads r-2 as the project and deletes everything recorded after it, which includes the third rotate's log entry and any later chat.

So yes, it works as expected across close and reopen, with one specific limit: manual edits are individually reversible only while the session is open. After reopen, the restore points are exactly the chat messages.

content.text: Does your design mean that now there are two mechanisms to track operations such as rotation or move? If that's the case, it's not very error-prone. For example, if the user restored to a point in the history, what will happen if the user presses undo ?  In the past, you are freaking bad at referencing the same thing with multiple names. And by doing so, you confuse yourself and me. Please stop doing that. Use consistent terminologies when you reference to any new concept that you're bringing up. And try and stay with plain English.

Short answer: there is one thing that detects edits, one record derived from it, and one stash of full project files. After a Revert, Undo does nothing, on purpose. Let me fix the vocabulary first, then answer both questions with only these four terms.

**Terms, used from here on and nothing else.**
- **Undo history**: OrcaSlicer's built-in undo and redo. Lives in memory only. Cleared when a project is opened, created, or reverted. This exists today with or without JusPrin.
- **Change log**: JusPrin's saved list of lines like "rotate, by you, 15:02". Saved in the project. Holds no model data.
- **Copy**: a full project file JusPrin saves so it can go back to that moment. What I earlier also called a checkpoint, snapshot, or revision. One word from now: copy.
- **Revert**: the timeline's "Revert here" action. Distinct from OrcaSlicer's Undo button.

**Are there two mechanisms tracking a rotate?** No. Only the undo history detects anything. The change log does not watch for rotates itself. It watches the undo history: each time the undo history gains a step, the change log writes one line describing it. So the change log cannot disagree with the undo history about what happened, because it is copied from it. The two differ in one intended way: the undo history is memory only and is trimmed when it gets large, while the change log is saved with the project and kept. That is the whole reason the change log exists. Copies are separate from both. A copy is taken when a chat message is sent, and it does not care how the change log or undo history got there.

**Revert, then Undo.** Today's code loads the chosen copy as if it were a freshly opened project and clears the undo history. I verified this in the restore function ([OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:396](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:396)). So after a Revert, pressing Undo does nothing, exactly as after opening a project. The design keeps that. It is the coherent choice because Revert also permanently deletes everything after that point, meaning later chat, later change log lines, and later copies. If Undo could bring the model back to its pre-revert state, the model would be back but its history would be gone, and the timeline would be lying.

**What the design must do at that moment.** The change log keeps a bookmark into the undo history, meaning the last step it has already written a line for. Whenever the undo history is cleared, that bookmark resets. This happens at three moments, all already present in OrcaSlicer: open a project, start a new project, Revert. One rule, three triggers, and it is unit-testable. The existing guard that keeps the restore itself from being logged as a stream of edits stays.

**The other interaction worth knowing.** Undo across a message boundary, without any Revert: you rotate, send a message, which takes a copy, then press Undo. The undo history still has the rotate, so Undo works. The change log writes a new line, "undo rotate", after the message. The copy taken at the message still holds the rotated state, which is correct: that is what the project looked like when the message was sent. The timeline stays truthful and the restore points are unchanged.

So the risk is not two trackers fighting. The risk is forgetting to reset the bookmark at one of the three clearing moments, which is a single rule to implement and test.

Are you saying that the undue history is the source of truth and the changelog is derived value?  If so,  When the project is closed and reopened, the undue history will be lost from the memory, right? Are you trying to build a system where the source of truth will by default be gone? That sounds like the most ridiculous design I've ever heard. Try to explain to me how your design holds water using plain English. For complex problems like this, you need to cut to the cord of the problem. And once you have done that, you will arrive at a very solid design. And that solid design usually can be explained concisely using plain English. You need to learn this from human beings, you know.

No. I said it badly. The undo history is not the source of truth for anything in this design. It is only the trigger. Here is the design in plain terms.

**There are two questions the timeline has to answer, and each has its own durable answer.**

1. What did the project look like at this point? Answered by a copy: a full project file saved at that moment. Copies are saved inside the project. They are the source of truth for going back. Nothing about going back depends on the undo history.

2. What happened between those points? Answered by the change log: a line written the instant an edit happens, saved inside the project. The change log is the source of truth for history. Once a line is written, nothing depends on where the signal came from.

**The undo history's only job is to say "an edit just happened."** OrcaSlicer already fires it for every real edit, with its own rule for what counts as real. JusPrin listens to that signal and writes a change log line at that moment. That is the whole use. It is never read back later. This is how every log in the world works: the event is transient, the log is permanent. Losing the undo history at close loses nothing, because everything it was needed for was already written down when it happened.

**Why that trigger and not another.** The alternative is JusPrin placing its own "something changed" call at every edit site in OrcaSlicer. Today there are about twenty, they miss half the edits, and each one is a rebase conflict forever. The undo history is one signal that OrcaSlicer itself maintains for every edit, so JusPrin gets completeness for free and touches OrcaSlicer in one place.

**Close and reopen, checked against that.** The change log is in the file, so the timeline shows exactly what happened. The copies are in the file, so Revert to any message works. The undo history is empty, so Undo is empty. That last part is identical to vanilla OrcaSlicer, which loses all undo on close. JusPrin adds restore points on top and takes nothing away.

**Where it can break, honestly.** Only at write time. If JusPrin misses the signal for an edit, the change log is missing a line. That is bounded by OrcaSlicer's own rule for real edits, which it already relies on for its unsaved-changes marker. And the one bookkeeping rule from before: when the undo history is cleared, JusPrin's bookmark into it resets.

Your other objection, that saving full copies is wasteful, is separate and still stands. It is about how much a copy costs, not about what is the source of truth. I owe you an answer on that, and OrcaSlicer's own auto-backup, which writes each object's mesh once and only rewrites it when the mesh changes, is the likely basis for a cheaper copy. I'll lay that out next if you want it.
So can I think of a copy as the entire project file minus mesh (unless mesh changes)? If so, lay out the cheaper copy using orca's auto-backup
I need to read OrcaSlicer's auto-backup code precisely before laying this out, since the design would lean on it. Checking what it writes, when, and how a backup is loaded back.

content.text:
Yes, that is the right mental model, and OrcaSlicer's own auto-backup already writes exactly that. I read the code; here is what it does and how a cheaper copy sits on top of it.

**Three terms for this message.** Thin file: a project file with everything except meshes. Mesh file: one object's geometry, in OrcaSlicer's own per-object format. Mesh store: a JusPrin folder holding mesh files, each named by the hash of its content. The other terms stay as before: copy, change log, undo history, Revert.

## What OrcaSlicer's auto-backup does today

OrcaSlicer keeps a backup folder for every open project and maintains two things in it, on its own, whether JusPrin exists or not.

- **Mesh files, written only when a mesh changes.** Whenever an object's geometry or paint changes, OrcaSlicer writes that one object's mesh file into the backup folder on a background thread. The triggers are already in place: add or delete a part, replace a mesh, split, add a primitive, a paint stroke for supports, seams, or color, a part-level move, and any undo or redo that changes geometry. Moving or rotating a whole object does not touch the mesh file, because instance positions live in the thin file.
- **A thin file, every ten seconds when something changed.** It holds the object list, every instance position and rotation, per-object settings, plates, the project settings, the embedded presets, custom G-code by height, and a reference to each object's mesh file by id. It skips meshes, thumbnails, G-code, and the auxiliary folder.
- **Crash restore reassembles them.** After a crash, OrcaSlicer loads the thin file with its restore mode, which pulls each mesh from the mesh files beside it. This is a shipped path that users exercise.

## The cheaper copy

A copy becomes a thin file plus a short list: for each object, which mesh file it used.

- **Taking a copy, at a message boundary as before.** Write a thin file into the JusPrin folder using OrcaSlicer's backup save mode. Then, for each object, hash its current mesh file; if that hash is not in the mesh store yet, put the file there once. Record the object-to-hash list with the copy in the state file. A rotate, move, or settings change costs a thin file only. A painting session costs one new mesh file per painted object per copy, not per stroke. An import or cut costs one new mesh file.
- **Revert.** Build a temporary folder holding the thin file and the mesh files it references, copied out of the mesh store under the names the thin file expects. Load it with OrcaSlicer's restore mode, exactly as crash restore does. Clear the undo history as today.
- **Growth.** The project file grows by one mesh file per changed object, and by tens of kilobytes per copy otherwise. A project with two hundred messages and one painted object holds that object's mesh once per copy where its paint changed, and nothing else grows with the mesh.
- **Cost at Send.** The thin file is the same writer minus the mesh part, and the mesh part was the entire difference between 7 ms and 1.7 s in the earlier measurements. I have not measured the thin file itself. My expectation is tens of milliseconds regardless of mesh size, which would make the worker-thread work in the copy-cost handoff unnecessary. That number should be measured before committing.

## What has to be solved, honestly

1. **Pending mesh writes.** OrcaSlicer writes mesh files asynchronously and has no "wait until done" call. JusPrin must not hash a file that is still being written. The clean fix is one small additive function in the backup manager that waits for its queue to drain. That is one OrcaSlicer touch point.
2. **File names embed the object name.** A copy must record the name each object had at that time so Revert can recreate the expected file name. Straightforward, but it must be tested with renames.
3. **The restore call.** Today's Revert loads a full file. It needs a variant that loads a folder in restore mode, and restore mode also sets the project filename, which must be handled.
4. **Cleanup.** When Revert deletes later copies, mesh files no copy references anymore are deleted from the mesh store.
5. **Backup must be on.** OrcaSlicer enables it at startup in the GUI; verify JusPrin never turns it off.

If you want, the next step is to measure the thin file with the existing harness and then rewrite the copy-cost handoff around this design instead of the worker thread.

# Handoff: spike to validate thin copies for the revision timeline

Written 2026-09-10 on branch `jusprin-newui` at commit `64193984ed`. This is a
spike, not an implementation task. Its output is a yes-or-no answer to the
questions in "What the spike must answer", with evidence, plus a recommendation.
Companions: `revision-timeline-handoff.md` (when copies are taken and why),
`revision-copy-cost-handoff.md` (what a full copy costs and the worker-thread
alternative this spike may make unnecessary).

## Terms

Use these words and no others for these things.

- **Copy**: what the timeline saves so "Revert here" can go back to a moment.
  Today a copy is a full project file, meshes included.
- **Thin file**: a project file with everything except meshes: object list,
  instance positions and rotations, per-object settings, plates, project
  settings, embedded presets, custom G-code by height, and a reference to each
  object's mesh file. OrcaSlicer's auto-backup already writes one
  (`SaveStrategy::Backup`, `src/libslic3r/Format/bbs_3mf.hpp:143`).
- **Mesh file**: one object's geometry and paint in OrcaSlicer's per-object
  format, named `3D/Objects/<object name>_<backup id>.model`. OrcaSlicer's
  auto-backup writes one whenever an object's mesh or paint changes
  (`_BBS_3MF_Exporter::save_object_mesh`, `bbs_3mf.cpp:5978`).
- **Mesh store**: a JusPrin folder of mesh files, each named by the hash of its
  content, so an unchanged mesh is stored once.
- **Manifest**: the short list saved with a copy: for each object, the mesh
  file name the thin file will look for, and the hash of the mesh file it
  needs.
- **Materialize**: turn a copy back into something OrcaSlicer can load: the
  thin file plus the mesh files it references, laid out as OrcaSlicer expects.
- **Revert**: the timeline's "Revert here". Distinct from OrcaSlicer's Undo.

## The problem this spike exists for

A full copy re-serializes every triangle. Measured in the shipping build: about
0.8 s of frozen UI for a 20 MB mesh and 1.8 s for 50 MB, and the project file
grows by the whole mesh at every copy. Kenneth's reaction: saving duplicate
copies of unchanged meshes is wasteful. The obvious alternative is a copy that
carries the meshes by reference and stores each mesh once.

## The candidate design, stated as small as it can be

1. A copy is a thin file plus a manifest.
2. The mesh store holds mesh files named by content hash. A mesh file is written
   only when its hash is not already in the store.
3. Taking a copy, on the UI thread at a conversation boundary: write the thin
   file with OrcaSlicer's backup save mode; for each object, compute the hash
   of the mesh file it would produce; write that mesh file into the store if
   the hash is new; write the manifest.
4. Revert: materialize the copy into a folder, then load it with OrcaSlicer's
   crash-restore mode (`LoadStrategy::Restore`, `Plater.cpp:12185-12235`),
   the same shipped path that restores an unsaved project after a crash. Then
   clear the undo history, as today.
5. One invariant: every hash in every manifest exists in the mesh store.
   Check it after every copy and before every Revert. A failed check is an
   error, shown as a revision with no checkpoint, never a silent fallback.

Everything else is an existing OrcaSlicer call. JusPrin owns exactly two
pieces of logic: how the hash is computed, and materialize.

## Can we claim this is obviously correct? Honest answer

No. Not for the whole feature, and not today.

The full-copy design can make that claim. It has one file per copy and one
call to load it. Its cost is what rules it out, not its correctness.

The thin design adds references, and references can dangle or point at the
wrong content. Two things can go wrong, and only two: the hash fails to
change when the mesh file would have changed, so an old mesh is silently
reused; or materialize lays the files out differently from what OrcaSlicer's
restore expects. Neither is obvious by inspection, because both depend on the
contents of two OrcaSlicer functions, the mesh file writer and the restore
loader.

What can be made obvious is smaller than the feature and is the target of
this spike:

- **The hash must cover exactly what the mesh file writer reads.** The writer
  is one function (`_add_mesh_to_object_stream` and the object stream around
  `bbs_3mf.cpp:7300-7345`, which writes vertices, triangles, per-volume
  transforms, and the four kinds of paint per triangle). If the spike lists the
  fields that function reads, and the hash is defined as a hash over exactly
  that list, then "hash unchanged means file unchanged" is checkable by reading
  two lists side by side, and testable by mutating each field once.
- **Materialize must be a pure function of stored files**, with a single
  equivalence test as its definition of correct: for any project state,
  loading materialize(copy(state)) must give the same project as loading
  full_export(state). Same object count, same mesh hashes, same instance
  transforms, same per-object settings, same paint, same plates, same project
  settings. If that test passes across the edit matrix below, materialize is
  correct for every case the matrix covers, and the matrix is the explicit
  boundary of the claim.
- **The invariant check runs in production.** A dangling reference is caught
  when the copy is taken, not when someone tries to revert a week later.

That is the path toward "so simple there are obviously no errors": shrink
what JusPrin decides to two functions, define each by an equivalence against
OrcaSlicer's own save and load, and keep the full-copy design as the fallback
if either equivalence cannot be shown. The spike's job is to find out whether
the two equivalences hold, and how cheaply.

## What the spike must answer

Each question has a pass criterion. Answer all of them, with numbers or
evidence, even if an early one fails.

**Q1. What does a thin file cost?** Time `Plater::export_3mf(path,
SaveStrategy::Backup)` on the UI thread at 2k, 100k, 400k and 1M triangles in
the Release build, three runs each, with file sizes. Pass: under 100 ms at 1M
triangles. (A measurement of this was started on 2026-09-10 with the harness
described under "Existing assets"; use its numbers if they exist.)

**Q2. What exactly is in a mesh file, and can a cheap in-memory hash cover it?**
Read the writer and list every model field it reads. Define the hash over that
list. Then, for each field, mutate it once and confirm the hash changes and the
mesh file bytes change; mutate something outside the list (instance position,
object rename, a process setting) and confirm the hash does not change and the
mesh file bytes do not change. Pass: every mutation inside the list changes
both; every mutation outside changes neither. Report the hash cost at 1M
triangles.

**Q3. Does a mesh file need an OrcaSlicer touch point to write synchronously?**
The public `Slic3r::save_object_mesh` queues an asynchronous write into the
project's backup folder with no way to wait for it (`_BBS_Backup_Manager`,
`bbs_3mf.cpp:8591`). Find the smallest additive change that lets JusPrin write
one object's mesh file to a path of its choosing, on the calling thread, and
say what it is. Pass: a one-function addition, or a way to do it with no
change at all. Read `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md` before proposing
any OrcaSlicer edit.

**Q4. Does materialize plus restore give the same project as a full export?**
Build the equivalence test. For each state in the edit matrix: take a full
export, take a thin copy, materialize it, load both into fresh projects, and
compare. Pass: identical on every compared property for every row.

**Q5. Can materialize produce a single full project file instead of a folder,
so Revert keeps today's load path unchanged?** The thin file is a zip that
already references `3D/Objects/<name>.model` entries it did not include. If
those entries can be added to the zip and the result loads as an ordinary
project, then the restore path needs no change at all and the design gets
simpler. Pass: yes, with a working test; or no, with the reason.

**Q6. Do hashes survive close and reopen?** Open a saved project, take a copy
without editing, and check whether every hash matches the stored files. If
serialization is not deterministic across sessions, the store grows by one
mesh file per object per session. Pass: hashes match. If not, report the
growth and whether it is acceptable.

**Q7. Cleanup.** After Revert deletes later copies, mesh files no manifest
references must be deleted. Define the rule and show it in the test. Pass:
no orphan files after a revert; no referenced file ever deleted.

## Edit matrix for Q2 and Q4

Every row is one project state to save both ways and compare. Start from a
loaded sphere or the 20 mm test cube in `tests/data/test_stl/`.

| Row | Edit | Why it is here |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | No edit | Baseline |
| 2 | Move an instance | Must not touch the mesh file |
| 3 | Rotate an instance | Same |
| 4 | Rename the object | Changes the mesh file name, not its content |
| 5 | Paint supports on a few triangles | Paint lives in the mesh file |
| 6 | Paint seam; paint color; paint fuzzy skin | The other three paint kinds |
| 7 | Move a part inside the object | Per-volume transform lives in the mesh file |
| 8 | Add a modifier; add a negative volume | Volume types |
| 9 | Change a per-object setting | Lives in the thin file |
| 10 | Change a process setting; switch a filament | Lives in the thin file |
| 11 | Add custom G-code at a height from the slider | Lives in the thin file |
| 12 | Two objects, then cut one | New meshes |
| 13 | Two objects sharing one mesh (duplicate) | `ShareMesh` behavior |
| 14 | Two plates with one object each; plate settings changed | Plates |
| 15 | Delete an object | Manifest shrinks |
| 16 | Save, close, reopen, no edit | Q6 |

Compare, for each row: object count and names; per object, the mesh file hash
after loading; instance transforms; per-object and per-volume settings; the
serialized paint for each volume; plate assignments and plate settings; the
project settings; custom G-code entries.

## Existing assets

- **Benchmark harness**: `export_bench_harness.cpp`, currently in a session
  scratch folder (`/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/8fb7ea15-3027-4bc1-a582-9c286517984f/scratchpad/`;
  if that folder is gone, the earlier copy is in
  `.../28d33b5a-3e97-48b6-8eaf-5192f6d7d30d/scratchpad/`). It boots the real
  GUI, loads a generated sphere at a chosen triangle count, and times exports.
  Modeled on `tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp`. It is built by
  temporarily appending an `add_executable` block to
  `tests/workspace/CMakeLists.txt` linking `libslic3r_gui`; the block is in
  the copy-cost handoff. Build with `--config Release`; the RelWithDebInfo
  configuration is compiled at `-O0` (`CMakeLists.txt:544-548`) and its timings
  are 4.5 times too high. If the spike keeps the harness, it belongs under
  `tests/workspace/` behind a manual target.
- **Release build** of `libslic3r_gui` exists under `build/arm64`.
- **Measurements so far** (Release, one object, one plate): full export 40 ms
  / 243 ms / 822 ms / 1.77 s at 2k / 100k / 400k / 1M triangles; copy file
  89 KB / 1.2 MB / 4.6 MB / 9.3 MB. Details in the copy-cost handoff.
- **OrcaSlicer code to read first**: the backup manager and its tasks
  (`bbs_3mf.cpp:8591-8900`), the mesh file writer (`:5978`), the object
  stream writer (`:7300-7345`), the thin-file save flags
  (`save_model_to_file`, `:5930-5945`, and every `m_skip_static` check), the
  restore loader (`:1403-1412`, `:1687-1697`), Plater's crash-restore call
  (`Plater.cpp:5412-5430`), the load path (`:12185-12235`), and the triggers
  that call `save_object_mesh` (`Model.cpp:521,1250-1389`, `Model.hpp:703,1210`,
  the painting gizmos, `GLCanvas3D.cpp:4981,5107,5200,5309`).

## What the spike must not do

- Do not build the feature. No changes to `ProjectPersistence`,
  `ProjectStateDocument`, the bridge, or the Agent page.
- Do not commit OrcaSlicer changes. If Q3 needs one, write it as a patch file
  with the fork-stewardship evidence and leave it uncommitted.
- Do not touch the change log or undo history parts of the timeline design.
  This spike is only about what a copy is made of.

## Deliverable

One document, `agent-docs/jusprin/revision-thin-copy-spike-result.md`, with:

1. A table of Q1 through Q7 with pass or fail and the evidence.
2. The field list from Q2 and the hash definition.
3. The equivalence test's source location and how to run it.
4. The proposed OrcaSlicer change from Q3, if any, as a patch.
5. A recommendation: adopt thin copies, adopt full copies on a worker thread,
   or a third option the spike found. If thin copies: which questions are
   still open and what the implementation must add beyond the spike.

And a rewrite of the "Decision" section of the copy-cost handoff to match.

Boots the real `GUI_App` with an isolated data dir, maximizes, selects the 3D editor, waits for GL init, then per size generates a sphere with `its_make_sphere`, writes it as STL, loads it via `load_files`, settles 5 event-loop turns, then runs: thin export (UI thread) x3, `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::export_project_archive` x3, mesh file x3, hash x3, round trip x1. - Built with the temporary CMake block, `--config Release`, target `export_bench_harness`; binary at `build/arm64/tests/workspace/Release/JusPrinExportBench.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinExportBench`. The first build recompiled all 700 `libslic3r_gui` objects (9 min), so Release was not fully up to date before; the results are from the fresh Release library.

- `export_3mf` refuses any path not ending in `.3mf` (Plater.cpp:15721), so thin files are named `thin-<triangles>-<run>.3mf` and the restore file is literally `.3mf`.

**Brief report on the thin file.**

The thin file costs about 10 ms and 15 KB no matter how big the mesh is. In the same optimized build, a full copy costs 1.75 s and 9.3 MB at one million triangles. The design question you asked, "copy = whole project minus meshes unless a mesh changed," holds.

| Mesh | Thin file | Full copy | One mesh file | Hash a mesh file |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2k triangles | 12 ms | 37 ms | 9 ms | 0.3 ms |
| 100k triangles | 12 ms | 240 ms | 230 ms | 7 ms |
| 400k triangles | 7 ms | 815 ms | 805 ms | 28 ms |
| 1M triangles | 7 ms | 1.75 s | 1.75 s | 56 ms |

**The round trip works.** At all four sizes the harness rotated the object, wrote a thin file, put the mesh file beside it, wiped the project, and loaded the pair back through OrcaSlicer's crash-restore path. Object count, triangle count, name, and the 45 degree rotation all came back intact. No new loader code was needed.

**Two facts that shape the implementation.** OrcaSlicer's mesh writer deliberately waits 3 seconds after the last edit before writing, and it runs on its own thread with no way to ask "are you done." So at a message boundary the mesh file on disk may be stale or half-written. Writing a mesh file costs the same as a full export, but only for objects whose mesh or paint changed, and only when that happened. And after a restore-mode load, OrcaSlicer treats the folder it loaded from as its own backup folder and deletes it later, so Revert must always work from a throwaway folder, never from the mesh store.

**What this means for the design.** For moves, rotates, and settings changes, which are most edits, a copy at Send drops from about a second to about 10 ms plus a hash. The remaining cost is concentrated in one place, the mesh file for a changed object, and that is the one question the spike still has to settle: write it on the UI thread at Send, or wait for OrcaSlicer's writer. The spike handoff now records the Q1 result, the partial Q4 result, and both facts.

Yes. It removes the hardest part entirely, and I checked the three facts it depends on. It does not remove everything, and one thing it keeps is a real limitation.

**What goes away.** No copies at all: no thin files, no mesh store, no manifest, no rebuilding files for a restore, no project file growth, no dependence on OrcaSlicer's background mesh writer, and no reopen story. In their place, two calls into machinery that every Undo click already exercises:

- At each message, JusPrin takes a marker in the undo history: an ordinary undo step with a "!" name, which OrcaSlicer's own rule treats as "not an edit," so it never counts as a change. The marker pins the exact state at that moment.
- Revert becomes "jump the undo history to that marker." OrcaSlicer already does this for its undo menu; the timestamp-based jump is private today and needs a small public wrapper. A jump restores objects, positions, rotations, parts, paint, plates including plate settings, and the wipe tower, because all of that is in the undo snapshot. I verified the plate list is serialized with each plate's settings.

**What the undo history does not hold, verified.**

1. Printer, filament, and process settings. An undo jump does not touch them. Reverting an Agent turn that changed settings must also put the settings back, so JusPrin records the settings at each marker and reapplies them on Revert. This is small, data only, and JusPrin already has the code that applies settings changes. But it means Revert is two actions, jump plus reapply, and they must succeed together.
2. Custom G-code set from the preview slider. Not in the undo snapshot. Either record it with the settings or accept that Revert does not undo it. It is rare.
3. Memory trimming. When the undo history exceeds one tenth of RAM or 1 GB, whichever is smaller, OrcaSlicer drops the oldest steps outright. Each distinct mesh is stored once, so moves and rotates are cheap, but painting stores per-triangle data for every stroke. A long painting session on a big model can push old markers out, and their Revert buttons must then honestly disappear. The limit is settable and JusPrin could raise it, at the cost of memory.

**Your premise, checked.** "Before the project is closed there is always an undo history" is true except for the trimming above, and except that OrcaSlicer clears it on new project, open project, and a Revert itself. So Revert is offered only for markers taken since the project was opened in this session, and after a Revert only for markers before it. That matches what you proposed.

**Is it obviously correct?** Closer than anything so far, because JusPrin owns no file format and no restore loader. What JusPrin owns fits in one list: take a marker and a settings record at each message; on Revert, jump and reapply; when a marker has been trimmed, show that. Everything else is OrcaSlicer's existing undo, tested by every user every day.

**What you give up.** No Revert after reopen. The timeline still shows the full history, since the change log is saved with the project, but earlier messages have no Revert button.

I would take this as the first version. The change log and the message boundaries are identical to the earlier design, so if cross-session Revert is ever wanted, thin copies can be added later as a second kind of restore point without touching anything else.
